abstract: The "Neurons for Today, Genes for Tomorrow model" (NTGT) predicts how the brain's neural and molecular control systems interact to regulate biological embedding, whereby social experience alters the brain to shape future behavior. We report here on the first test of this model, using honey bee queen retinue pheromone (QRP) and behavioral, single-nucleus transcriptomic, and electrophysiological analyses. Consistent with theory, weaker exposure triggered a simple attraction response and transcriptomic changes primarily in the antennal lobes (AL), whereas stronger exposure induced transcriptomic changes in the mushroom bodies, a brain region affecting more complex behavior. In addition, AL electrophysiological responses to QRP were enhanced after stronger exposure, also consistent with theory. We also showed how individual differences in biological embedding can be explained by NTGT, with individual differences in brain gene regulatory network topology, especially in specific sensory cell clusters, supporting a new mechanistic framework for behavioral regulation.
